# Quicx

> Quicx is a task queue daemon written in C for devices and servers with little memory. You give it a memory budget at startup; it never uses more, and when the budget is full it keeps the most valuable work: a task can evict a less valuable waiting task, but only when its allocator proves the freed memory fits the new one. As far as its author found, no other task queue does this.

Quicx runs a single-threaded event loop (epoll/kqueue) on top of apool, an adaptive page allocator: the budget is mapped once, and 16 KiB pages go to whichever block sizes the traffic sends and come back when they empty. A task is one block, a 64-byte record with its payload behind it. Tasks carry a value level from 0 to 15; workers get the highest level first, and level 15 is never evicted. Clients speak QXP, the Quicx Protocol, its own compact binary protocol (6-byte header, 13 message types). There is a Java client, dev.quicx:quicx-client, on Maven Central. Current version: 2.1.0. Started on 2 April 2026 by Dimitar Anastasov; open source under MIT.

## Measured (Quicx 2.0 and 2.1)

Measured with scripts in the repository on an Apple M4 Pro (macOS, arm64) and an Intel Core i3-2100 (2 cores / 4 threads, Ubuntu 24.04). Every number has a script and raw output next to it (docs/README.md in the repository maps them).

- Value-aware admission, real daemon, 256 KiB budget, one worker slower than the flood: 100 % of valuable tasks done under steady overload against 31.6 % for a queue that refuses new tasks; a valuable task waits 4.1 ms instead of 3.5 s. Evicting the oldest instead also keeps them in steady overload but evicts ten times as many tasks and loses 35 % of valuable ones in a burst.
- Capacity: 46,593 tasks of 100 B in the default 8 MiB, the same on both machines and exactly what the capacity formula gives. A daemon built with make MAX_PAYLOAD=8192 holds 1,002 tasks of 8,000 B in 8 MiB, again exactly the formula.
- Several daemons: on the i3, two daemons pinned to two cores did 35,000 tasks/s against 18,200 for one (1.92x); filling one of ten daemons left the other nine untouched.
- Throughput and latency: 81,900 tasks/sec end to end on one thread on the M4 Pro, 49 µs median, 98 µs p99; 19,000 tasks/sec on the i3.
- Memory: 1,056 KB idle, 9,088 KB with the queue full, 2,080 KB after the burst drains (macOS phys_footprint).
- Size: 36 KB on a Raspberry Pi (Linux arm64 release binary), no runtime dependencies, about 3,200 lines of C.
- Tests: 155 unit checks and 27 end-to-end checks, passing on macOS arm64 and Linux x86-64.

## Research

A simulation of the admission rule with ten ways of learning a task's value from worker scores (bandits, Thompson sampling, logistic regression, reinforcement learning) shows learning helps where value has a visible cause: logistic regression with regular probes analysed 2.4 times more valuable frames on a robot workload and doubled useful work on a ten-customer server; learning without exploration did worse than no learning. Learned value is the planned next step for eviction.

## Limitations

Quicx is an in-memory broker, not a durable one. No persistence (a restart empties the queue), no redelivery if a worker dies mid-task, no retries or dead-lettering, no delayed or named queues. Payloads are at most 1,024 bytes by default (up to 16,320 with a custom build). One daemon uses one core; run one per core. No hard real-time deadlines. Delivery is at-most-once; for at-least-once delivery, use beanstalkd or Redis Streams.

## Docs
- [Installation](https://quicx.dev/docs/installation): one-line install, checksums, pinning a version
- [Quick start](https://quicx.dev/docs/quick-start): first daemon, producer and worker
- [Configuration](https://quicx.dev/docs/configuration): every setting, the admission rule, capacity planning
- [Architecture](https://quicx.dev/docs/architecture): how a task moves through the daemon
- [Allocator](https://quicx.dev/docs/allocator): apool, its ideas from the allocator literature, and their measured effect
- [QXP Protocol](https://quicx.dev/docs/binary-protocol): frame header, message types, SUBMIT_VALUED
- [Benchmarks](https://quicx.dev/docs/benchmarks): measured results on two machines, value-aware admission, several daemons
- [CLI reference](https://quicx.dev/docs/cli-reference): start, stop, status, version, several daemons per machine
- [Java client](https://quicx.dev/docs/java-client): dev.quicx:quicx-client
- [Limitations](https://quicx.dev/docs/limitations): what Quicx does not do
- [Changelog](https://quicx.dev/docs/changelog): what changed in each release
